1177.title: the Samkhya Karika)
1177.hook: a spoonful of yesterday's curd in warm milk, and the yogurt that was already there
1177.howItsDone: Students of Indian philosophy learn the debate over causation, Samkhya's view that the effect pre-exists in its cause against the Nyaya-Vaisheshika view that it is newly made, as a long-running argument between the schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika reasoned its way to the witness: a bed is made for a sleeper outside it. A new week begins.
screen: `A BED FOR SOMEONE.` · `THE EFFECT IN THE CAUSE.`

segments.voice: Late at night in a kitchen, someone warms a pot of milk, lets it cool until it's just warm to the finger, and stirs in a spoonful of yesterday's curd. A lid goes on. The pot goes somewhere quiet. By morning, it's yogurt. Nobody added yogurt to it. Nobody built it. And the same trick does nothing to a pot of water. So where was the yogurt last night? Samkhya has a bold answer to that question, and it uses the answer to explain the whole universe. Today the Samkhya Karika argues about cause and effect.
screen: `MILK, A SPOON OF CURD, A NIGHT.` → `NOBODY BUILT THE YOGURT.` → `WHERE WAS IT LAST NIGHT?`

segments.voice: Samkhya's answer: the yogurt was already in the milk. Not visible, not yet set, but there. The effect exists in its cause before it shows itself. The Karika gives its reasons in one tight verse, and the verse ends with the claim itself, sat karyam: the effect already is. That's why the view is called satkarya. What doesn't exist at all can't be produced. You need the right material to start with. Not everything comes from everything. A cause can only produce what it's capable of. And the effect has the same nature as its cause. Commentators reach for examples like these: press sesame seeds and you get oil, press sand all day and you get none. The oil was in the sesame. If effects are already hidden in causes, then the whole world was already folded inside prakriti, the root. Creation, for Samkhya, isn't making something out of nothing. It's unfolding, the way the yogurt unfolds from the milk, and Samkhya teachers add that the world can fold back in again. Not every school agrees. Nyaya and Vaisheshika, the schools just before Samkhya, argue that a pot is a genuinely new thing that didn't exist before the potter made it. The two sides argued it out at length, and Hindu tradition keeps both arguments in the room. Samkhya's view also changes how a beginning looks. A seed, a child, a first draft. Whatever comes out of them, Samkhya would say, is already in there, waiting for its conditions.
screen: `THE EFFECT IS ALREADY IN THE CAUSE.` · `ONE VERSE, A STRING OF REASONS.` · `CREATION AS UNFOLDING.` · `NYAYA SAYS: THE POT IS NEW.`

segments.voice: Feel how each in-breath already holds the out-breath that will follow it, for a few rounds. Then bring to mind one beginning in your life right now, a project, a friendship, a habit, a child, and look at it the way Samkhya looks at milk: already holding what it will become, needing only time and warmth. If you pray, you can hold that beginning in prayer.
The Samkhya Karika. Its argument on causes: the effect already exists in its cause, so the world unfolds from prakriti instead of appearing from nothing.
Your line: the Samkhya Karika. A beginning already holds what it will become. See you tomorrow.

1178.title: the Samkhya Karika)
1178.hook: two travelers left behind in a forest, one who can't walk and one who can't see
1178.howItsDone: Teachers of Samkhya and of Yoga philosophy explain the meeting of purusha and prakriti with the story of the lame man and the blind man, drawn from the Karika's phrase and its commentaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika argued that the effect is already in its cause: yogurt in the milk, oil in the sesame.

A caravan has been scattered in a forest, and two travelers are left behind. One can't walk. The other can't see. Night is coming. The one who can't walk can see the path, the river, the way out, but he can't take a step. The one who can't see has strong legs and a strong back, but he has no idea which way to go. Alone, both of them stay in the forest. The classic commentaries on the Samkhya Karika tell this little story, and the Karika itself names it in a single phrase. Today it explains how the whole world got moving.
screen: `A CARAVAN SCATTERED.` → `ONE CAN'T WALK, ONE CAN'T SEE.` → `ALONE, BOTH STAY LOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the ending. The traveler who can't see lifts the other onto his shoulders. Now one does the walking and the other does the seeing, and together they get out of the forest. Once they reach the village, they go their separate ways. The Karika uses this picture for the two from Samkhya's opening days. Prakriti is the one with legs: she moves, changes and unfolds, but she has no seeing of her own. Purusha is the one with eyes: the witness, who sees but never acts. Their coming together, the verse says, is like the lame and the blind, and creation unfolds from that meeting. And the Karika says what the meeting is for. It's so that purusha can see prakriti, and so that purusha can finally be set free. In Samkhya the world isn't an accident, and it isn't a trap someone built. The whole unfolding, the gunas, the I-maker, the senses, the elements, is a journey with a purpose, and the purpose is seeing clearly. Notice too how the story ends. The two travelers part ways. That's where Samkhya is heading, and the next two days get there. Not everyone in the Hindu tradition tells the end of the journey this way. Vedanta, at the close of this season, has its own account. For now, the picture is enough. A partnership that neither side could manage alone, that gets somewhere, and then lets go.
screen: `ONE CARRIES, ONE GUIDES.` · `PRAKRITI MOVES, PURUSHA SEES.` · `A MEETING WITH A PURPOSE.` · `THE TRAVELERS PART WAYS.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your knee, lift it a little and lower it again, a few times: the hand is the one with legs, and it moves. Then notice the seeing, aware of the movement without lifting anything, and let the hand go still: let the body carry, let the seeing see. If you pray, you can offer thanks for the body that carries you.
The Samkhya Karika. Its picture of the world's beginning: prakriti, who moves but can't see, and purusha, who sees but can't move, getting out of the forest together.
Your line: the Samkhya Karika. One carries, one guides, and together they get out. That's today, done.

1179.title: the Samkhya Karika)
1179.hook: the ankle bells go quiet and the dancer leaves the stage: Samkhya's picture of the world's show
1179.howItsDone: The dancer image from the Samkhya Karika is taught in Samkhya and Yoga study as a picture of liberation through discernment.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika gave two travelers: prakriti, who moves but can't see, carrying purusha, who sees but can't move.

The last rhythm of a classical dance recital. The drummer's hands slow. The dancer strikes her final pose, ankle bells ringing, then still. For a moment nobody in the hall moves. Then she bows, and walks off the stage. She doesn't come back out to do it all again for the same people. The dance was for them, it was seen, and it's finished. The Samkhya Karika reaches for exactly this scene near its end, when it tries to say what happens once the world has done what it came to do.
screen: `THE FINAL POSE.` → `SHE BOWS AND WALKS OFF.` → `SEEN, AND FINISHED.`

segments.voice: The verse goes like this, in paraphrase. As a dancer stops dancing once she has shown herself to the audience, so prakriti stops, once she has shown herself to purusha. Hold yesterday's travelers in mind. Prakriti carried the seer through the forest so that purusha could see. The whole unfolding, everything in the count, has been a performance with one audience in view. The Karika adds two more touches. First, prakriti is generous. She serves purusha in many ways, the text says, and asks nothing back. Purusha does nothing in return; it can't. It only watches. Second, prakriti is modest. The Karika says nothing is more modest than she is. Once she knows she has been truly seen, she doesn't show herself to that seer again. And a few verses later the text gives the last exchange, almost like a play. One says, I have seen her, and loses interest. The other says, I have been seen, and stops. That's Samkhya's picture of freedom, and notice what it isn't. It isn't fighting the world, or escaping it, or hating it. It's seeing it so completely that its hold just ends, the way a song you've finally understood stops replaying in your head. The dance isn't wasted. It was the whole point, right up until the bow. Tomorrow, on the last day of Samkhya: what the seer is left with.
screen: `THE DANCER STOPS WHEN SEEN.` · `PRAKRITI IS GENEROUS.` · `PRAKRITI IS MODEST.` · `I HAVE SEEN HER. I HAVE BEEN SEEN.`

segments.voice: Pick one sound, a breath, a hum in the room, a car going by, and stay with it from its first edge to its last, letting it finish completely. Then wait, quiet, until something else steps onto the stage, and watch that one to its end too. If you pray, you can offer each ending as it comes.
The Samkhya Karika. Its picture of freedom: prakriti as a dancer who, once truly seen, finishes her dance and leaves the stage.

1180.title: the Samkhya Karika)
1180.hook: who, exactly, needs to be set free? the Samkhya Karika's last surprise
1180.howItsDone: In Samkhya and Yoga study, the closing verses of the Karika on bondage, release and kaivalya are read with commentaries, and the image of the crystal beside a colored flower is used to explain how the witness only seems to be affected.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika's dancer, once truly seen, finished and left the stage.

Who, exactly, needs to be set free? A freedom story usually comes with a prisoner. Someone locked up, someone chained, someone who walks out at the end and blinks in the sunlight. A teaching about release has to meet the same question: release of whom, and from what? For days now, Samkhya has been building toward its answer. Purusha the witness, prakriti the dancer, the long count of principles in between. Today, on the last day with the Samkhya Karika, it gives its answer, and the answer is a surprise.
screen: `WHO NEEDS TO BE SET FREE?` → `RELEASE OF WHOM?` → `SAMKHYA'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the surprise, in paraphrase. No one, the Karika says, is really bound. No one is really released. No one really wanders from life to life. It is prakriti, in her many forms, who is bound, who wanders and who is released. Remember where the line sits. The I-maker, the mind, the feelings of being stuck, all sit on prakriti's side. Purusha, the witness, was never in chains. It only seemed to be, the way a clear crystal seems red when a red flower sits beside it. Freedom isn't the witness breaking out. It's the confusion clearing up. And how does it clear? The Karika says it comes from practicing the principles, the twenty-four in the count, again and again, until a knowledge arises that it describes in three short steps: I am not, nothing is mine, not I. That isn't despair. It means that thinking, owning and the sense of me all belong to prakriti, and the witness stops claiming them. What's left, the Karika says, is a knowledge that's pure and complete. Its name for the goal is kaivalya, aloneness: the seer standing on its own. Look back over these days. The I-maker that says mine. The count, named. A bed made for a sleeper. Yogurt already in the milk. Two travelers. A dancer's bow. And now the seer, alone and free. Tomorrow, a return to Yoga, the darshana that takes this map and turns it into a practice.

The Samkhya Karika. Its last word on freedom: the witness was never bound. Prakriti is bound and released, and the seer is left alone, kaivalya.

1181.title: Yoga (revisited)
1181.hook: two hikers, one trail map: Samkhya studies it, Yoga laces up its boots
1181.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga darshana read Patanjali's Yoga Sutra with its classical commentary attributed to Vyasa, and practitioners in a number of lineages take up its eight limbs, from ethics and posture to meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Samkhya Karika closed: the witness was never really bound, and the seer stands alone, kaivalya.

Two friends have the same trail map spread across a kitchen table. One of them traces every contour line, names every peak, learns where each stream comes from and where it goes. The other folds the map into a pocket and starts lacing up her boots. They aren't arguing. They're using the same map in two ways. For ten days this path has read Samkhya's map: the seer, the seen, the strands, the count. Today, the darshana that took that map and laced up its boots. It's come up before on this path. Now it returns as a school: Yoga.
screen: `ONE MAP, TWO FRIENDS.` → `ONE STUDIES, ONE WALKS.` → `YOGA, AS A SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: The root text of the Yoga darshana is the Yoga Sutra, credited by tradition to Patanjali. Read it right after the Samkhya Karika and the furniture looks familiar. The Sutra speaks of the seer and the seen. It says the seen is made of the three gunas, light, activity and inertia, and of the elements and the senses. It says the seen exists for the seer's sake, for experience and for release. That's Samkhya's map, nearly line for line. But the Sutra asks a practical question: how do you get the confusion to clear? Its second verse answers: yoga is the stilling of the movements of the mind. And the next verse says what happens then. The seer rests in its own nature. That's the crystal from yesterday, with the red flower moved away. Then Yoga adds two things of its own. First, a whole program of practice: ethics, posture, breath, withdrawing the senses, concentration, meditation, absorption. Second, Ishvara, a special purusha untouched by affliction and karma, and the Sutra offers devotion to Ishvara as one path to stillness. The Samkhya Karika says nothing of Ishvara, and the schools are allowed to differ. And one verse speaks right to the dancer's bow. For the one whose seeing is complete, the Sutra says, the seen has ended, but it hasn't ended for everyone else, because it's shared. The dance goes on for the rest of the audience. So Yoga isn't stretching with a philosophy attached. It's Samkhya's map, walked.
screen: `THE SAME MAP: SEER AND SEEN.` · `STILLING THE MIND'S MOVEMENTS.` · `YOGA ADDS PRACTICE AND ISHVARA.` · `THE DANCE GOES ON FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, and give the mind one thing to rest on: the feel of the breath at the nostrils. Each time it moves, to a plan, a sound, a memory, notice and come back, not forcing anything still, just letting the movements settle the way water clears when no one stirs it. If you pray, you can rest in Ishvara, or whatever you pray to, as the Sutra allows.
Yoga. As a darshana, the school of Patanjali's Yoga Sutra: Samkhya's map of seer and seen, walked through practice, with room for Ishvara.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. Still water lets the seer rest in its own nature. Until tomorrow.

1182.title: Yoga (revisited)
1182.hook: a weather report for the mind: Vyasa's five grounds, from scattered to stilled
1182.howItsDone: Students of Yoga philosophy read the Yoga Sutras together with Vyasa's commentary, and teachers often use his five grounds of the mind to help a student see where their attention is before they begin to practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yoga as a school: Samkhya's map, walked, stilling the mind's movements so the seer can rest.

A weather report never calls the sky good or bad. It says what's up there. Clear. Overcast. Gusts. Fog rolling in by evening. Nobody gets angry at the forecaster for mentioning the fog; it's just useful to know what you're walking into. The Yoga Sutras come down to us with a commentary attached, credited by tradition to a sage named Vyasa. And in his very first comment, before the work has properly begun, Vyasa gives a weather report for the mind. Five kinds of sky.
screen: `A WEATHER REPORT.` → `NO GOOD SKY, NO BAD SKY.` → `FIVE SKIES OF THE MIND.`

segments.voice: The first sutra only says that the teaching of yoga begins now. Vyasa opens his comment on it with a short line: yoga is samadhi, the settled, absorbed mind. Then something easy to miss. Samadhi, in some form, is a quality of the mind in every one of its grounds. And he names the grounds. Kshipta, the scattered mind, thrown in every direction. Mudha, the dull mind, heavy and fogged over. Vikshipta, the distracted mind, which settles now and then but keeps getting pulled away. Ekagra, the one-pointed mind, resting on a single thing; this path met it back in year two. And niruddha, the stilled mind, where the turnings have quieted. Here's the honest part. Vyasa says the steady moments of a distracted mind don't count as yoga yet, because the distraction swallows them. Yoga proper, for him, belongs to the one-pointed and the stilled. That's strict. But read it as a report, not a grade. The list doesn't sort people into good and bad. It describes skies, and one person can pass under several of them before lunch. Samkhya gave us the gunas: light, motion and weight. Some readers of Yoga hear those three strands in these grounds: the restless one, the heavy one, the clear one. That's what makes Yoga a school and not just a set of exercises. It takes a map seriously enough to ask where you are on it, right now. Not, why can't I focus. Just, which sky is this?
screen: `YOGA IS SAMADHI.` · `FIVE GROUNDS OF THE MIND.` · `STEADY MOMENTS AREN'T ENOUGH YET.` · `A REPORT, NOT A GRADE.`

segments.voice: First, just check: is the mind racing, heavy, or coming and going? Name it once, without arguing, then rest on one thing, the feel of your hands in your lap, and when attention drifts, notice which sky pulled you away and come back. If you pray, you can rest on a name you pray with instead.
Yoga. In Vyasa's first comment, yoga is samadhi, and the mind has five grounds: scattered, dull, distracted, one-pointed and stilled.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. The mind has weather, and Vyasa reads it without blame. See you tomorrow.

1183.title: Yoga (revisited)
1183.hook: an angry reply, half typed, and Patanjali's advice for the thought that wants to hit send
1183.howItsDone: In the Yoga Sutras, the counsel to cultivate the opposite sits right after the restraints, such as non-harm, and the observances, and students of Yoga philosophy practice it both in quiet reflection and in the moment a harmful thought arises.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Yoga, Vyasa's five grounds of the mind: scattered, dull, distracted, one-pointed and stilled. A report, not a grade.

The reply is already half typed. Somebody in the group thread took credit for her idea, in front of everyone, and her thumbs are moving faster than her judgment. Every sentence is sharper than the last. The cursor blinks next to the send arrow. And there's a small gap, maybe a second long, where the hand hovers. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras have a line about that hovering second, the moment before.
screen: `THE REPLY, HALF TYPED.` → `THE HAND HOVERS.` → `ONE SECOND BEFORE.`

segments.voice: The line comes just after Patanjali lists the restraints, beginning with non-harm, and the observances. A list doesn't always stop a mood, and the next line meets that. In paraphrase: when you're troubled by thoughts that pull against these, cultivate the opposite. The Sanskrit name is pratipaksha bhavana, cultivating the other side; this path first met it in year two. Then the next sutra takes the harmful thought apart. It may be done by you, or you may get someone else to do it, or you may just approve of it. It may come from greed, from anger or from confusion. It may be mild, middling or intense. Whichever it is, the sutra says, it ends in endless pain and not knowing. Seeing that, you cultivate the opposite. Notice what this isn't. It isn't, think happy thoughts. The opposite starts by following the angry thought honestly to where it leads, and seeing the cost. Approving counts too: a cheer from the sidelines sits in the same list as the blow. Vyasa's commentary pictures someone tempted to harm stopping to remember why they took up yoga at all, and how foolish it would be to pick back up what they had already put down. That's the week, in small. Samkhya counted what's on the screen and found the witness watching it. Vyasa named the weather. Now Patanjali shows what to do when the weather turns to storm: not fight it, not obey it, but turn the thought around and look at its other side.
screen: `CULTIVATE THE OPPOSITE.` · `DONE, CAUSED OR APPROVED.` · `FOLLOW IT TO WHERE IT LEADS.` · `FROM COUNTING TO TURNING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small, recent irritation, nothing raw, and let the sharp thought arrive. Without scolding it, follow it a few steps ahead, if I said it, then what, and notice the cost; then let its other side come up, patience, fairness or simple quiet, and rest there for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold the person you were annoyed with in prayer.
Yoga. In Patanjali's sutras, when a harmful thought arrives, yoga means cultivating its opposite, pratipaksha bhavana.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. In the second before sending, a thought can be turned around. Same time tomorrow.
